subject: physics

items.q: Two insulating materials are rubbed against each other. Which statement describes what happens?
items.correct: Electrons are rubbed off one material and on to the other one.
items.misconception: Rubbing creates fresh charge on the surface of each material.
items.why: Students meet friction first as a way of producing heat, and the phrase 'produce static electricity' sounds like producing something new. Nothing visible moves during the rubbing, so the transfer is easy to miss. Rubbing only moves electrons about. Count them: every electron the cloth loses is an electron the rod gains, so the two charges always appear together and are equal in size. If charge were being created, one object could end up charged on its own, and that never happens.
items.random_wrong: Protons are rubbed off one material and on to the other.

items.q: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth. The rod becomes negatively charged. What has happened to the cloth?
items.correct: It has lost electrons to the rod, so it is now positively charged.
items.misconception: It has gained some protons from the rod, so it is positively charged.
items.why: A student who sees a positive charge appear assumes that positive particles must have travelled to make it. Protons and electrons are often taught as an equal-and-opposite pair, so they seem equally free to move. Protons are locked inside the nuclei of the atoms and cannot be rubbed off a surface. Only the outer electrons are loosely enough held to move. A positive charge is what is left behind when electrons leave, not something that arrives.
items.random_wrong: It has lost all of its charge, so it now has no charge at all.

items.q: Why is the positive charge left on one rubbed material always equal in size to the negative charge on the other?
items.correct: Every electron lost by one is an electron gained by the other.
items.misconception: Rubbing always produces equal amounts of the two charges at once.
items.why: Students meet friction first as a way of producing heat, and the phrase 'produce static electricity' sounds like producing something new. Nothing visible moves during the rubbing, so the transfer is easy to miss. Rubbing only moves electrons about. Count them: every electron the cloth loses is an electron the rod gains, so the two charges always appear together and are equal in size. If charge were being created, one object could end up charged on its own, and that never happens.
items.random_wrong: Both of the materials are rubbed with exactly the same steady force.

items.q: A student rubs a metal rod held in her bare hand with a dry cloth. The rod shows no sign of being charged. Why not?
items.correct: Charge on the rod flows away through her hand and body.
items.misconception: Metal cannot gain or lose any electrons when it is rubbed.
items.why: Charging by rubbing is demonstrated with rods that look ordinary, so students treat it as a property of rubbing rather than of the material. The word 'insulating' in the specification is easy to skip over. The specification says certain insulating materials. Charge stays put on an insulator, but a metal conducts, so charge produced on a hand-held metal rod immediately leaks away through the person to earth. Held on an insulating handle, the same metal rod does keep its charge.
items.random_wrong: Rubbing a smooth metal surface is unable to create any charge.

items.q: Two charged objects are brought close together but do not touch. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Two objects that carry the same type of charge repel each other.
items.misconception: Two objects with the same type of charge attract each other.
items.why: The first demonstrations of static electricity are attractions - a charged rod picking up paper or bending a stream of water - so students generalise that charge means attraction. Test it with two rods charged in the same way, which must carry the same type of charge: hung on a thread, they swing apart. Like repels like, unlike attracts.
items.random_wrong: The objects only push or pull when their surfaces touch.

items.q: Two polythene rods are each rubbed with the same dry cloth. One rod hangs freely on a thread. The second rod is held close to it, without touching. What happens, and why?
items.correct: The hanging rod swings away, because both carry a like charge.
items.misconception: The hanging rod swings away, because rubbing magnetised them.
items.why: Magnetism is the student's only earlier example of a non-contact push and pull, so a new non-contact force is filed under the label they already have. Rubbing moves electrons; it does not magnetise anything. Polythene and acetate are not magnetic materials at all, and a charged rod attracts small pieces of paper, which no magnet will do.
items.random_wrong: The hanging rod swings towards it, because charges attract.

items.q: Which observation is the best evidence that charged objects exert forces on one another when they are not in contact?
items.correct: A hanging charged rod turns away as a like charge is put near.
items.misconception: A charged rod picks up small pieces of paper when it touches them.
items.why: Everyday forces are contact forces - pushing, pulling, hitting - so a force acting across empty space feels like it needs an explanation the student does not yet have. The suspended rod starts turning before the second rod reaches it, and it keeps turning while a visible gap remains. The force is already acting across that gap.
items.random_wrong: A rubbed plastic rod picks up small iron filings from a nearby dish.

items.q: A charged polythene rod repels a second charged polythene rod. A student says this shows that rubbing has magnetised the rods. Why is the student wrong?
items.correct: The force is electrostatic; rubbing only moves electrons.
items.misconception: Magnets repel across a gap, so the two effects must be the same.
items.why: Magnetism is the student's only earlier example of a non-contact push and pull, so a new non-contact force is filed under the label they already have. Rubbing moves electrons; it does not magnetise anything. Polythene and acetate are not magnetic materials at all, and a charged rod attracts small pieces of paper, which no magnet will do.
items.random_wrong: Magnetism can only act when two poles are brought into contact.

items.q: A student walks across a nylon carpet and then feels a small shock as her hand nears a metal door handle. What has happened?
items.correct: Friction charged her up, and charge then crossed the air as a spark.
items.misconception: The carpet made new charge, which was stored in the metal handle.
items.why: Students meet friction first as a way of producing heat, and the phrase 'produce static electricity' sounds like producing something new. Nothing visible moves during the rubbing, so the transfer is easy to miss. Rubbing only moves electrons about. Count them: every electron the cloth loses is an electron the rod gains, so the two charges always appear together and are equal in size. If charge were being created, one object could end up charged on its own, and that never happens.
items.random_wrong: Charge jumps from her hand only once her skin has touched it.

items.q: Charge builds up on an object until a spark suddenly jumps across a gap to a nearby earthed metal pipe. Why does the spark happen?
items.correct: The field grows strong enough for the air in the gap to conduct.
items.misconception: Air can never conduct, so the light must come from the metal pipe.
items.why: Air is introduced as a good insulator with no exceptions given, so a current in air seems impossible and the light has to be explained some other way. Air is an insulator only up to a point. A strong enough field pulls electrons off the air particles so that the air conducts, and the flowing charge makes the flash and the crack you hear.
items.random_wrong: Charge can only cross a gap at the moment two surfaces touch.

items.q: Two acetate rods are each rubbed with a dry cloth and both become positively charged. In terms of electrons, why do the rods then repel each other?
items.correct: Each rod lost electrons to its cloth, so the like charges repel.
items.misconception: Each rod gained protons from its cloth, so both are now positive.
items.why: A student who sees a positive charge appear assumes that positive particles must have travelled to make it. Protons and electrons are often taught as an equal-and-opposite pair, so they seem equally free to move. Protons are locked inside the nuclei of the atoms and cannot be rubbed off a surface. Only the outer electrons are loosely enough held to move. A positive charge is what is left behind when electrons leave, not something that arrives.
items.random_wrong: Rubbing made positive charge on each rod, which pushes them apart.

items.q: What is an electric field?
items.correct: A region in which a charge experiences a force.
items.misconception: A set of paths that a charged object has to follow.
items.why: The lines are drawn as solid, continuous marks, which look like tracks. Students have also seen circuit diagrams, where lines really are wires that carry charge. The lines are a way of drawing the field on paper; nothing runs along them. They tell you which way the force points and, by how closely they are packed, how strong the field is.
items.random_wrong: Only the lines drawn around a charge on a diagram.

items.q: How does the strength of the electric field around a charged sphere change as you move further away from the sphere?
items.correct: It gets weaker; the field is strongest close to the charged sphere.
items.misconception: It gets stronger, because the field spreads out as it goes out.
items.why: The lines fan out and cover more paper further away, which students read as the field growing rather than thinning out. Further out, the same number of lines is spread over a larger area, so the lines are further apart and the field is weaker. That is why a spark jumps across a small gap and not a large one.
items.random_wrong: It stays the same up to the last line and then stops there.

items.q: A charged object is moved closer to a second charged object. What happens to the force between them?
items.correct: The force gets stronger as the distance between them decreases.
items.misconception: The force stays the same, as it depends only on the two charges.
items.why: The charge is the quantity written on the diagram and talked about in class, so it becomes the only variable the student thinks the force can depend on. The second object sits in the first object's field, and that field is strongest close in. Move the objects closer and the field there is stronger, so the force is stronger too.
items.random_wrong: The force gets weaker, because the two fields start to cancel.

items.q: Which description matches the electric field pattern that should be drawn for an isolated charged sphere?
items.correct: Straight lines spreading out from the sphere in all directions.
items.misconception: Circles drawn all the way round the sphere, all evenly spaced out.
items.why: Students confuse the electric field pattern with contour lines on a map, or with the loops of a magnetic field pattern around a bar magnet. The force on a charge near a sphere points straight towards or straight away from the centre, so the lines must be radial. A circle would mean the force pushed a charge round the sphere, which it does not.
items.random_wrong: Straight lines that always point inwards, towards the sphere itself.

items.q: How does the idea of an electric field help to explain the force between two charged objects that are not touching?
items.correct: Each object sits in the other's field, so each feels a force.
items.misconception: Each object sends out lines that pull the other one along them.
items.why: The lines are drawn as solid, continuous marks, which look like tracks. Students have also seen circuit diagrams, where lines really are wires that carry charge. The lines are a way of drawing the field on paper; nothing runs along them. They tell you which way the force points and, by how closely they are packed, how strong the field is.
items.random_wrong: The objects interact only if a field line joins one to the other.

items.q: A rubbed polythene rod is negatively charged and the cloth that rubbed it positively charged. They are held close but not touching. What happens?
items.correct: They attract each other across the gap.
items.misconception: They repel each other across the gap.
items.why: Sharing to equalise is the rule students learn for heat and for water levels, so they apply the same rule to charge. Charge only spreads out where it can flow, which means on a conductor. On an insulating rod it stays on the part that was rubbed, which is why one end can attract paper while the other does not.
items.random_wrong: The forces cancel out, so neither moves.

items.q: Are the two charges produced by rubbing always the same size?
items.correct: Yes. The charge lost by one material is exactly the charge gained by the other, so the two are equal in size and opposite in sign.
items.misconception: One material ends up more strongly charged than the other, depending on how hard it was rubbed or what it is made of.
items.why: Rubbing feels one-sided, because the student holds one object and moves the other, so it seems as though something is done to one object and not the other. Every electron that leaves one surface arrives on the other, so the counts must match. Rubbing harder transfers more electrons, but it increases both charges together and by the same amount.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which way do the arrows point on the field lines around a charged sphere?
items.correct: Away from a positive sphere and towards a negative sphere, showing the force on a positive charge.
items.misconception: The arrows always point inwards towards the charged object, because a field pulls things in.
items.why: Gravitational field diagrams are met first and always point inwards, and the word 'field' is remembered as something that attracts. The arrow shows which way a positive test charge would be pushed. Next to a positive sphere it would be repelled, so the arrows point outwards; only a negative sphere has arrows pointing in.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is there a field in the gaps between the lines on a field diagram?
items.correct: Yes. The field fills the whole region around the charged object; the lines are only a way of drawing it.
items.misconception: The field only exists along the lines, so a charge sitting in a gap would feel no force at all.
items.why: The diagram shows a small number of separate lines, so the empty paper between them looks like empty space with nothing in it. You could draw as many lines as you like; drawing more does not add field. A charge placed anywhere near the sphere feels a force, so the field is everywhere around it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When can charge cross the gap between a charged object and an earthed one?
items.correct: Charge can cross a gap of air as a spark, before the two ever touch.
items.misconception: Charge can only move across at the moment the two surfaces actually touch each other.
items.why: Charge is usually taught as something that flows through a conductor, and air is taught as an insulator, so a gap looks like a complete barrier. The shock from a door handle happens as your hand approaches it, not after contact, and the spark is visible in the gap. A strong enough field lets charge cross the air.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is the spacing of the field lines around a charged sphere chosen?
items.correct: Lines are drawn closer together where the field is stronger, which is close to the sphere.
items.misconception: The lines get closer together the further you move away from the sphere.
items.why: Students remember that spacing means something without remembering which way round it goes, and lines that meet in the distance look like a familiar perspective drawing. Close spacing means a strong field. The field is strongest at the surface, so the lines are packed most tightly there and spread further apart as they go out.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the field stop at the last line drawn on the diagram?
items.correct: No. The field keeps getting weaker with distance but does not have an edge where it ends.
items.misconception: The field reaches as far as the longest line on the diagram and then stops completely.
items.why: A diagram has to stop somewhere, and the student reads the edge of the drawing as the edge of the field. The lines are cut short only to fit on the page. Further out the field is too weak to matter, but there is no distance at which it switches off.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
